\chapter{How Are You?}
\label{ch:pt-how-are-you}
\hlchaptermodality{2}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask a Portuguese speaker how they are, casually or respectfully, and answer for myself.}

The full Chapter 2 exchange: greet, ask Tudo bem?, answer for yourself, and hand the question back. PT-C02-formal-practice then rebuilds the same exchange for respect (Como está o senhor?), so the chapter's canDo covers both registers.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[de nada]{de nada — \textquotedblleft{}you're welcome,\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}it was nothing\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:PT-C02-de-nada}



\begin{quote}
You already say \textbf{obrigado / obrigada} (\textquotedblleft{}I am obliged\textquotedblright{}). The reply that closes the exchange is \textbf{de nada} — \textquotedblleft{}of nothing\textquotedblright{} — the very same phrase, word for word, as Spanish.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{final-a-reduces} — \textbf{de nada} $\approx$ \emph{dee NAH-duh}: unstressed final \emph{-a} softens toward \emph{uh}; the \emph{d} is soft.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{de} = \textquotedblleft{}of / from\textquotedblright{} (Latin \textbf{dē}).
  \item \textbf{nada} = \textquotedblleft{}nothing\textquotedblright{} — and it has the same buried story as its Spanish twin.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{nada} comes from Latin \textbf{(rēs) nāta}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}a born thing\textquotedblright{}} — from \emph{nāscī}, \textquotedblleft{}to be born\textquotedblright{} (English \textbf{nat}ive, \textbf{nat}ure, \textbf{nat}al, re-\textbf{nais-sance}). Latin \emph{nōn … rēs nāta}, \textquotedblleft{}not a single born thing,\textquotedblright{} wore down until the \textquotedblleft{}born thing\textquotedblright{} word, \textbf{nada}, came to mean \textbf{nothing} by itself.

Portuguese and Spanish inherited the identical word and the identical courtesy:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}you're welcome\textquotedblright{}} & \textbf{the \textquotedblleft{}nothing\textquotedblright{} word} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Portuguese} & \emph{de nada} & \emph{nada} $\leftarrow$ \emph{nāta}, \textquotedblleft{}a born thing\textquotedblright{} \\
\textbf{Spanish} & \emph{de nada} & \emph{nada} $\leftarrow$ \emph{nāta}, \textquotedblleft{}a born thing\textquotedblright{} \\
\textbf{French} & \emph{de rien} & \emph{rien} $\leftarrow$ \emph{rem}, \textquotedblleft{}a thing\textquotedblright{} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So Iberia says \textquotedblleft{}of no \emph{born-thing}\textquotedblright{}; France says \textquotedblleft{}of no \emph{thing}.\textquotedblright{} Same shrug of the shoulders, one Latin idea.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}obrigado / obrigada\textquotedblright{} … \textquotedblleft{}de nada\textquotedblright{} — the full exchange
  \item \textquotedblleft{}de nada\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}native, nature\textquotedblright{} — nada's true family
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{nada} originally mean in Latin? (A \emph{born thing} — \emph{nāta}.) Which language shares \emph{de nada} exactly, and which uses \emph{de rien} instead? (Spanish; French.) Next: \textbf{como}, \textquotedblleft{}how.\textquotedblright{}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[como]{como — \textquotedblleft{}how,\textquotedblright{} the fourth \emph{quomodo} cousin}

\label{lesson:PT-C02-como}



\begin{quote}
One of two everyday ways to ask \emph{how are you?} in Portuguese starts with \textbf{como}, \textquotedblleft{}how.\textquotedblright{} It's the same word you've met (or will meet) across the Romance family.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{final-o-is-u} — \textbf{como} = \emph{KOH-moo}: the final unstressed \emph{-o} is said like \emph{u}. (Portuguese does this to nearly every final \emph{-o}: \emph{obrigado} $\to$ \emph{-doo}.)
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{como} = \textquotedblleft{}how / like / as.\textquotedblright{} Root: Latin \textbf{quōmodo}, \textquotedblleft{}in what manner\textquotedblright{} — \emph{quō} (\textquotedblleft{}in what way\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{modo} (\textquotedblleft{}manner\textquotedblright{}). It is the \textbf{same source} as its siblings:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Spanish \textbf{cómo}, Italian \textbf{come}, French \textbf{comment} — all \textquotedblleft{}how.\textquotedblright{}
  \item Doubling as \textquotedblleft{}like/as,\textquotedblright{} it matches Spanish \emph{como}, Italian \emph{come}.
\end{itemize}

Notice Portuguese and Spanish look almost identical here — \emph{como} vs \emph{cómo} — the only visible difference is the Spanish written accent that marks the \emph{question}. Portuguese leans on context and the question mark instead. The \emph{modo} piece lives on in English \textbf{mode}, \textbf{mod}el, \textbf{mod}erate.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the two Portuguese \textquotedblleft{}how are you\textquotedblright{}s}]
Portuguese asks after you \textbf{two} ways, and you'll assemble both next lesson:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Como vai?} — \textquotedblleft{}how do you \textbf{go}?\textquotedblright{} (verb \emph{ir}, \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{} — like French/German).
  \item \textbf{Como está?} — \textquotedblleft{}how do you \textbf{stand/are}?\textquotedblright{} (verb \emph{estar} — like Spanish).
\end{itemize}

Plus a third, verb-free favourite — \textbf{Tudo bem?} — coming up.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}como\textquotedblright{} — \emph{KOH-moo}
  \item como / cómo / come / comment — the four \emph{quomodo} siblings
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Como vai?\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}Como está?\textquotedblright{} — go, and stand
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin word gives \emph{como}, and name two siblings. (\emph{quōmodo} $\to$ \emph{cómo}, \emph{come}, \emph{comment}.) What's the only written difference between Portuguese \emph{como} and Spanish \emph{cómo}? (The Spanish accent that marks a question.) Next: the word behind Portuguese's favourite greeting — \textbf{tudo}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tudo]{tudo — \textquotedblleft{}everything,\textquotedblright{} the heart of \emph{Tudo bem?}}

\label{lesson:PT-C02-tudo}



\begin{quote}
The most Brazilian way to greet someone doesn't use a \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} or a \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} at all — it just asks \textbf{Tudo bem?}, \textquotedblleft{}everything well?\textquotedblright{} To own it, learn its first word: \textbf{tudo}, \textquotedblleft{}everything.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{final-o-is-u} — \textbf{tudo} = \emph{TOO-doo}: final \emph{-o} $\to$ \emph{u}, and the \emph{d} is soft.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{tudo} = \textquotedblleft{}everything, all,\textquotedblright{} from Latin \textbf{tōtus}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}whole, entire.\textquotedblright{}} You ask whether the \textbf{whole} of someone's life is going well — \emph{is everything OK?}

That root \textbf{tōtus} is completely at home in English:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{total}, \textbf{totally}, \textbf{totality} — the whole amount.
  \item \textbf{teetotal} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{total}ly\textquotedblright{} abstaining (a playful reduplication of \emph{total}).
  \item Italian \textbf{tutto}, Spanish \textbf{todo}, French \textbf{tout} — the same \emph{tōtus} across the family (you'll hear Spanish \emph{todo} echoing this).
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: pairing it with \textquotedblleft{}well\textquotedblright{}}]
Portuguese \textquotedblleft{}well\textquotedblright{} is \textbf{bem} ($\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{bene}, \textquotedblleft{}well\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{bene} of \emph{bene}fit, \emph{bene}volent; cousin of Spanish \emph{bien}, French \emph{bien}). Put them together:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Tudo bem?} = \textquotedblleft{}Everything well?\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}How are you? / You OK?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The magic: \textbf{no pronoun, no verb.} You skip the whole \emph{você / tu / o senhor} tangle. That's why \emph{Tudo bem?} is the friendliest, safest opener in Brazilian Portuguese — and you can answer with the very same two words: \textbf{Tudo bem.} (\textquotedblleft{}Everything's well.\textquotedblright{}) Or just \textbf{Tudo bom.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tudo\textquotedblright{} — \emph{TOO-doo}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Tudo bem?\textquotedblright{} — everything well?
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tudo\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}total, totally\textquotedblright{} — one family
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin word gives \emph{tudo}, and its English cousins? (\emph{tōtus} $\to$ total, totally, teetotal.) Why is \emph{Tudo bem?} so easy to use? (No pronoun, no verb — it dodges the \emph{você/tu/senhor} choice.) What's Portuguese for \textquotedblleft{}well\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{bem} $\leftarrow$ \emph{bene}.) Next: assemble all three \textquotedblleft{}how are you\textquotedblright{}s.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Tudo bem?]{Tudo bem? — “everything well?”}

\label{lesson:PT-C02-tudo-bem}



\begin{quote}
You know \textbf{tudo}, “everything.” Add \textbf{bem}, “well,” and Portuguese gives you an everyday check-in with no verb at all.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Tudo bem?} — “Everything well?” / “How are you?”
\end{quote}

The friendly answer can be identical:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Tudo bem.} — “Everything’s well.”
\end{quote}

Because the question contains no “you” and no verb, it avoids choosing a social register. That simplicity is exactly why it is everywhere.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Add the listener only when useful}]
To bounce the question back, say:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Tudo bem, e você?} — “All well, and you?”
\end{quote}

Everyday \textbf{você} comes from \emph{vossa mercê}, “your mercy.” Centuries of fast speech wore a respectful title into the ordinary pronoun “you,” much as Spanish \emph{usted} grew from a form meaning “your grace.” For more explicit respect, Portuguese can use \textbf{o senhor / a senhora}, “the gentleman / the lady.”

You do not need either pronoun for the basic pair: \textbf{Tudo bem? — Tudo bem.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “Tudo bem?”
  \item the answer — “Tudo bem.”
  \item “Tudo bem, e você?”
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} “Tudo bem? — Tudo bem!”

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{Tudo bem?} literally ask? (“Everything well?”) Why can it fit almost any listener? (It has \textbf{no verb and no pronoun}.) How do you bounce it back? (\textbf{E você?}) Where did \emph{você} come from? (\emph{Vossa mercê}, “your mercy.”) Next: two questions that do use verbs.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Como vai? / Como está?]{Como vai? / Como está? — go and stand}

\label{lesson:PT-C02-como-vai-esta}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Tudo bem?} needs no verb. \textbf{Como} (“how”) also builds two familiar metaphors.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{question} & \textbf{literally} & \textbf{verb} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Como vai?} & “How does it \textbf{go}?” & \emph{ir}, to go \\
\textbf{Como está?} & “How do you \textbf{stand}?” & \emph{estar}, to be / stand \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Vai} comes from \emph{ir}, whose Latin ancestor \emph{īre} also sits inside English \emph{exit} and \emph{transit}. \textbf{Está} comes from Latin \emph{stāre}, “to stand.”

Portuguese therefore keeps both pictures:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the “go” family, like French and German;
  \item the “stand” family, like Spanish and Italian.
\end{itemize}

Italian also keeps both. You do not need those languages to speak Portuguese; the map simply makes the two metaphors memorable.

\textbf{Tudo bem?} remains the easiest default because it skips the verb and register choice altogether.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the verb-free question — “Tudo bem?”
  \item the “go” question — “Como vai?”
  \item the “stand” question — “Como está?”
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} “Tudo bem? — Como vai? — Como está?”

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which question has no verb? (\textbf{Tudo bem?}) Which uses “go”? (\textbf{Como vai?}, from \emph{ir}.) Which uses “stand”? (\textbf{Como está?}, from \emph{estar}.) Portuguese keeps how many metaphors? (\textbf{Both}.) Next: the “more or less” answer.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mais ou menos]{mais ou menos — the \textquotedblleft{}more or less\textquotedblright{} shrug}

\label{lesson:PT-C02-mais-ou-menos}



\begin{quote}
Someone asks \emph{Tudo bem?} You're okay-ish. The Portuguese shrug is \textbf{mais ou menos} — \textquotedblleft{}more or less\textquotedblright{} — the same words, root for root, that Spanish uses.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{nasal-ai} — \textbf{mais} $\approx$ \emph{mais} with a nasal glide (\emph{maish} in Brazil, the \emph{s} a soft \emph{sh}).
  \item \texttt{final-o-is-u} — \textbf{menos} $\approx$ \emph{MEH-noos}; \textbf{ou} = a closed \emph{oh}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{mais ou menos} = literally \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}more or less.\textquotedblright{}} Every piece is Latin at heart:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{mais} = \textquotedblleft{}more,\textquotedblright{} from Latin \textbf{magis} (\textquotedblleft{}more\textquotedblright{}) — cousin of \emph{major}, \emph{master}, \emph{maximum}, \emph{mayor}.
  \item \textbf{ou} = \textquotedblleft{}or,\textquotedblright{} from Latin \textbf{aut}.
  \item \textbf{menos} = \textquotedblleft{}less,\textquotedblright{} from Latin \textbf{minus} — the very word English borrowed for \emph{minus}, \emph{minor}, \emph{minimum}, \emph{minus}cule.
\end{itemize}

So \emph{mais ou menos} is a \textbf{word-for-word twin of Spanish \emph{más o menos}} — Iberia's shared shrug. (Portuguese \emph{mais} and Spanish \emph{más} are the same \emph{magis}; the nasal \emph{-ais} is just Portuguese's accent.)
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: your answer ladder for \emph{Tudo bem?}}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{answer} & \textbf{sense} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Tudo bem / Tudo ótimo} & all well / all great \\
\textbf{Mais ou menos} & so-so \\
\textbf{Mais ou menos} + a hand-wobble & \textquotedblleft{}eh, could be better\textquotedblright{} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The five-language shrug set is now complete: Portuguese/Spanish \textbf{mais/más o menos} (\textquotedblleft{}more or less\textquotedblright{}), Italian \textbf{così così} (\textquotedblleft{}so, so\textquotedblright{}), French \textbf{comme ci comme ça} (\textquotedblleft{}like this, like that\textquotedblright{}), German \textbf{es geht} (\textquotedblleft{}it goes\textquotedblright{}).
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mais ou menos\textquotedblright{} — with a little wobble
  \item answer \textquotedblleft{}Tudo bem?\textquotedblright{} two ways — \textquotedblleft{}Tudo bem!\textquotedblright{} / \textquotedblleft{}Mais ou menos\textquotedblright{}
  \item Portuguese \emph{mais ou menos} = Spanish \emph{más o menos}, same Latin \emph{magis}/\emph{minus}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{mais ou menos} literally mean? (\textquotedblleft{}More or less.\textquotedblright{}) What Latin words are \emph{mais} and \emph{menos} from, and their English cousins? (\emph{magis} $\to$ major/ maximum; \emph{minus} $\to$ minor/minus.) Which language's shrug is its exact twin? (Spanish \emph{más o menos}.) Next: put the whole exchange together.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — Tudo bem?, start to finish}

\label{lesson:PT-C02-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Assemble the chapter’s atoms into one casual exchange before adding the formal version.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\begin{quote}
— Olá! \textbf{Tudo bem?} — \textbf{Tudo bem, e você?} — \textbf{Mais ou menos.} — {[}after a small favour{]} Obrigado! — \textbf{De nada.}
\end{quote}

The glue is \textbf{e você?}, “and you?”: \textbf{e} continues Latin \emph{et}, while \emph{você} grew from the respectful title \emph{vossa mercê}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built: What you are retrieving}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{de nada} — “of nothing,” you’re welcome;
  \item \textbf{tudo bem?} — the verb-free check-in;
  \item \textbf{como vai? / como está?} — “go” and “stand” alternatives;
  \item \textbf{mais ou menos} — “more or less,” so-so.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the whole exchange, both voices
  \item answer with “Tudo bem”
  \item answer with “Mais ou menos”
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} “Tudo bem? — Tudo bem, e você?”

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Run the casual exchange without looking. Which phrase answers a small favour? (\textbf{De nada}.) Which answer means “so-so”? (\textbf{Mais ou menos}.) Which question is safest before choosing a register? (\textbf{Tudo bem?}) Next: rebuild the exchange with \textbf{o senhor / a senhora}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Formal practice — Como está o senhor?}

\label{lesson:PT-C02-formal-practice}



\begin{quote}
The casual exchange is secure. Now replace ordinary \emph{você} with the respectful title \textbf{o senhor} or \textbf{a senhora}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\begin{quote}
— Bom dia. \textbf{Como está o senhor?} — \textbf{Bem, obrigado. E o senhor?} — Tudo bem.
\end{quote}

For a woman, use \textbf{a senhora}. The words continue Latin \emph{senior}, “older,” the same root as English \textbf{senior} and Spanish \emph{señor}.

The verb stays \textbf{está} because the title is grammatically third person: “How is the gentleman/lady?” That respectful grammar is already packed into the phrase; do not switch it to informal second-person \emph{estás} here.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item to a man — “Como está o senhor?”
  \item to a woman — “Como está a senhora?”
  \item “Bem, obrigado. E o senhor?”
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} “Como está o senhor? — Bem, obrigado.”

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which titles mean a respectful “you”? (\textbf{O senhor / a senhora}.) Which verb form follows them? (\textbf{Está}, third person.) Where does \emph{senhor} come from? (Latin \emph{\textbf{senior}}, “older.”) You can now run the Chapter 2 exchange casually or formally.
\end{tcolorbox}
